questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
questions.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4,$ $q=-1$ and

$$
p+q=4+(-1)=3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
questions.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ 1 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(7-\lambda )+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+9I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+9I) & =O \\ A-8I+9{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{8}{9}I-\frac{1}{9}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{8}{9},$ $q=-\frac{1}{9},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{8}{9}+(-\frac{1}{9})=\frac{7}{9}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}14-\lambda  & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{10}$ | $+$ | $x$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-4\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{12}$ | $\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$ |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,4x$ |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\  & =2A-3I \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers
questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $\text{tr}(A)=-8$ and $\text{det}(A)=12.$ Then, ${A}^{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by 

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).
$$

Therefore, using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-\text{tr}(A)A+\text{det}(A)I & =O \\ {A}^{2} & =\text{tr}(A)A-\text{det}(A)I \\ {A}^{2} & =-8A-12I.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=-{\lambda }^{3}+5\lambda -12.$ Then, ${A}^{3}=$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ -{A}^{3}+5A-12I & =O \\ {A}^{3} & =5A-12I.\end{aligned}
$$
